An ink reservoir for an industrial printer can hold up to $150\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of ink solution with $18\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved ink dye. A more concentrated ink solution with concentration $\frac{4}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.

Since $Q$ is the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which ink dye enters the reservoir minus the rate at which ink dye leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which ink dye enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $\frac{4}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ of ink dye enters the reservoir at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *ink dye* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(\frac{4}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =12\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which ink dye exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which ink dye leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $9\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $6\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+9t-6t=3(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of ink dye in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ *ink dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=12.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 12 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =12(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =12(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 12(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =12\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of ink dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 4(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 80+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{20}^{2}} & =-62 \\ C & =-62(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(20+t)-\frac{62(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =4(20+t)-62{\left(\frac{20}{20+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $150\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=150$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =150 \\ 60+9{t}_{o}-6{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 60+3{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 3{t}_{o} & =90 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =4(20+30)-62{\left(\frac{20}{20+30}\right)}^{2} \\  & =200-62{\left(\frac{20}{50}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈190.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $240\,\text{L}$ of water; a solution enters at $16\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $24\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
240+16t-24t=(240-8t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $24\,\text{L/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(24\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{24Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{30-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.4-\frac{3Q}{30-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{30-t}Q=0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(30-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|30-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30-t)^{-3}} \\  & =(30-t)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30-t)^{-3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30-t)^{-3}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{30-t}Q) & =(30-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.4 \\ (30-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(30-t)^{-4}Q & =0.4(30-t)^{-3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30-t)^{-3}) & =0.4(30-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30-t)^{-3})\,dt & =\int 0.4(30-t)^{-3}\,dt \\ Q(30-t)^{-3} & =0.4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(30-t)^{-2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.2(30-t)+C(30-t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $9\,\text{kg}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=9,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =9 \\ C(30-0)^{3}+0.2(30-0) & =9 \\ C(30)^{3}+6 & =9 \\ C & =\frac{3}{{30}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.2(30-t)+\frac{3}{{30}^{3}}(30-t)^{3} \\  & =0.2\cdot 30\,\left(\frac{30-t}{30}\right)+3{\left(\frac{30-t}{30}\right)}^{3} \\  & =6\,(1-\frac{t}{30})+3{(1-\frac{t}{30})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of fertilizer enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *fertilizer* enters the tank is 

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer exits the tank.

To find the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

As a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$

$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of fertilizer in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *fertilizer* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{15+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{15+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q=9.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(15+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|15+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(15+t)-\frac{27(15)^{2}}{(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(15+t)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{\sqrt{2x-y}-4}{16-2x+y} & =\frac{\sqrt{2(7)-(-2)}-4}{16-2(7)+(-2)} \\  & =\frac{4-4}{16-14-2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{\sqrt{2x-y}-4}{16-2x+y} & =\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{(\sqrt{2x-y}-4)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)}{(16-2x+y)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{2x-y-16}{(16-2x+y)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =-\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{16-2x+y}{(16-2x+y)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =-\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{\cancel{16-2x+y}}{\cancel{(16-2x+y)}(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =-\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-y}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\lim_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-y}+4} & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(7)-(-2)}+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{16}+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{8}.$

$$

$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$

A disinfectant reservoir in a water treatment facility can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of disinfectant solution with $10\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved disinfectant. A more concentrated solution with concentration $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir minus the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of disinfectant enters the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *disinfectant* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =12.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $25\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $20\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+25t-20t=5(12+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{12+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12.5-\frac{4Q}{12+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q=12.5.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 4/(12+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡|12+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(12+t)^{4}} \\  & =(12+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(12+t)^{4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(12+t)^{4}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q) & =(12+t)^{4}\cdot 12.5 \\ (12+t)^{4}\frac{dQ}{dt}+4(12+t)^{3}Q & =12.5(12+t)^{4} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{4}) & =12.5(12+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{4})\,dt & =\int 12.5(12+t)^{4}\,dt \\ Q(12+t)^{4} & =12.5\cdot \frac{1}{5}(12+t)^{5}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.5(12+t)+\frac{C}{(12+t)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $10\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 2.5(12+0)+\frac{C}{(12+0)^{4}} & =10 \\ 30+\frac{C}{(12)^{4}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{12}^{4}} & =-20 \\ C & =-20(12)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.5(12+t)-\frac{20(12)^{4}}{(12+t)^{4}} \\  & =2.5(12+t)-20{\left(\frac{12}{12+t}\right)}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 60+25{t}_{o}-20{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 60+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =24\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(24) & =2.5(12+24)-20{\left(\frac{12}{12+24}\right)}^{4} \\  & =90-20{\left(\frac{12}{36}\right)}^{4} \\  & ≈89.8\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{100})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{100})}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$

Let $Q$ be the amount of dissolved substance in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. The amount entering minus the amount leaving gives
$$\frac{dQ}{dt}=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}.$$
The units of these rates are $\text{kg/min}.$

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which substance enters the tank.
$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{in}}&=(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot(24\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\\
&=(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot(24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\\&=0.96\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which substance exits the tank.
The volume is
$$V(t)=1200+24t-36t=(1200-12t)\,\text{L}.$$
The concentration is $\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\text{kg/L}.$ Hence,
$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{out}}&=(36\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\\
&=(36\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\\
&=\frac{36Q}{1200-12t}\,\text{kg/min}=\frac{3Q}{100-t}\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}&=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}\\&=0.96-\frac{3Q}{100-t}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus,
$$\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100-t}Q=0.96.$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.
This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:
$$\begin{aligned}I(t)&=e^{\int 3/(100-t)\,dt}\\&=e^{-3\ln|100-t|}\\&=e^{\ln (100-t)^{-3}}\\&=(100-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying both sides by $I(t)=(100-t)^{-3}$ yields
$$\begin{aligned}(100-t)^{-3}\cdot(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100-t}Q)&=(100-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.96\\
(100-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(100-t)^{-4}Q&=0.96(100-t)^{-3}\\\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-3})&=0.96(100-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}$$
Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$
$$\begin{aligned}\int\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-3})\,dt&=\int 0.96(100-t)^{-3}\,dt\\Q(100-t)^{-3}&=0.96\cdot\frac{1}{2}(100-t)^{-2}+C\\Q(t)&=0.48(100-t)+C(100-t)^{3}.\end{aligned}$$
Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.
The initial condition is $Q(0)=22.$ Thus,
$$\begin{aligned}0.48(100-0)+C(100-0)^{3}&=22\\
48+C(100)^{3}&=22\\C(100)^{3}&=-26\\C&=- \frac{13}{500000}.\end{aligned}$$
Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$
$$Q(t)=- \frac{12 t}{25} - \frac{13 \left(100 - t\right)^{3}}{500000} + 48.$$
Writing this in the supplied normalized form gives
$$Q(t)=48(1-\frac{t}{100})-26(1-\frac{t}{100})^{3}.$$
Finally, we have $\alpha=48,\beta=-26,$ and

Let $Q$ be the amount of dissolved substance in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. The amount entering minus the amount leaving gives
$$\frac{dQ}{dt}=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}.$$
The units of these rates are $\text{kg/min}.$

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which substance enters the tank.
$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{in}}&=(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot(36\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\\
&=(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot(36\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\\&=1.44\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which substance exits the tank.
The volume is
$$V(t)=1200+36t-48t=(1200-12t)\,\text{L}.$$
The concentration is $\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\text{kg/L}.$ Hence,
$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{out}}&=(48\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\\
&=(48\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\\
&=\frac{48Q}{1200-12t}\,\text{kg/min}=\frac{4Q}{100-t}\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}&=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}\\&=1.44-\frac{4Q}{100-t}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus,
$$\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{100-t}Q=1.44.$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.
This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:
$$\begin{aligned}I(t)&=e^{\int 4/(100-t)\,dt}\\&=e^{-4\ln|100-t|}\\&=e^{\ln (100-t)^{-4}}\\&=(100-t)^{-4}.\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying both sides by $I(t)=(100-t)^{-4}$ yields
$$\begin{aligned}(100-t)^{-4}\cdot(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{100-t}Q)&=(100-t)^{-4}\cdot 1.44\\
(100-t)^{-4}\frac{dQ}{dt}+4(100-t)^{-5}Q&=1.44(100-t)^{-4}\\\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-4})&=1.44(100-t)^{-4}.\end{aligned}$$
Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$
$$\begin{aligned}\int\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-4})\,dt&=\int 1.44(100-t)^{-4}\,dt\\Q(100-t)^{-4}&=1.44\cdot\frac{1}{3}(100-t)^{-3}+C\\Q(t)&=0.48(100-t)+C(100-t)^{4}.\end{aligned}$$
Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.
The initial condition is $Q(0)=10.$ Thus,
$$\begin{aligned}0.48(100-0)+C(100-0)^{4}&=10\\
48+C(100)^{4}&=10\\C(100)^{4}&=-38\\C&=- \frac{19}{50000000}.\end{aligned}$$
Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$
$$Q(t)=- \frac{12 t}{25} - \frac{19 \left(100 - t\right)^{4}}{50000000} + 48.$$
Writing this in the supplied normalized form gives
$$Q(t)=48(1-\frac{t}{100})-38(1-\frac{t}{100})^{4}.$$
Finally, we have $\alpha=48,\beta=-38,$ and
$$\alpha-\beta=48-(-38)=86.$$

$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

$$

$$

$$

$$

The feed concentration must use kilograms: $$
\displaystyle 60\,\text{g/L}\cdot\frac{1\,\text{kg}}{1000\,\text{g}}=0.06\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.06\,\text{kg/L}$ of the salt enters the tank at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =2.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $560\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{560}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{40Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{14}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =2.4-\frac{Q}{14}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}Q=2.4.
$$

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{14}\alpha =2.4\,⟹\,\alpha =33.6.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=33.6.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14}+33.6.
$$

Finally,  the amount of salt in the tank $2$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$

A coolant tank initially holds $625\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $13\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved additive.
A feed solution containing $30\,\text{g/L}$ of the additive is pumped into the tank at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of additive in the tank $6$ minutes after pumping begins.

The feed concentration must use kilograms: $$
\displaystyle 30\,\text{g/L}\cdot\frac{1\,\text{kg}}{1000\,\text{g}}=0.03\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Let $Q$ be the amount of additive in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which additive enters the tank minus the rate at which additive leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which additive enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.03\,\text{kg/L}$ of the additive enters the tank at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *additive* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.75\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which additive exits the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $625\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of additive in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{625}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min},$ *additive* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(25\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{625}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{625}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{25Q}{625}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{25}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.75-\frac{Q}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}Q=0.75.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/25},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{25}\alpha =0.75\,⟹\,\alpha =18.75.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=18.75.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/25}+18.75.
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $13\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved additive. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=13,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =13 \\ A{e}^{-0/25}+18.75 & =13 \\ A & =-5.75\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=18.75-5.75{e}^{-t/25}
$$

Finally,  the amount of additive in the tank $6$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
Q(6)=18.75-5.75{e}^{-6/25}≈14.23\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

$$

We start by rewriting this equation in differential form.

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

Starting from 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3+y{e}^{2xy}}{3y-x{e}^{2xy}},\end{aligned}
$$

we first multiply through by $(3y-x{e}^{2xy})\,\text{d}x$:

$$
(3y-x{e}^{2xy})\,\text{d}y=(3+y{e}^{2xy})\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we then rearrange the terms:

$$
(3+y{e}^{2xy})\,\text{d}x+(x{e}^{2xy}-3y)\,\text{d}y=0
$$

Now, we should check for exactness. A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

For our differential equation, we have

$$
P(x,y)=3+y{e}^{2xy},\,Q(x,y)=x{e}^{2xy}-3y.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3+y{e}^{2xy}) \\  & ={e}^{2xy}+2xy\,{e}^{2xy}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{2xy}-3y) \\  & ={e}^{2xy}+2xy\,{e}^{2xy}\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,✓
$$

 

Thus, our equation is exact.

Since the equation is exact, our solution $u(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂x}=P(x,y),\,\frac{∂u}{∂y}=Q(x,y)
$$

First, we integrate $P(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+f(y) \\  & =\int (3+y{e}^{2xy})\,\text{d}x+f(y) \\  & =3x+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2xy}+f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate $Q(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$  Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y+g(x) \\  & =\int (x{e}^{2xy}-3y)\,\text{d}y+g(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2xy}-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we see that we must have

$$
g(x)=3x,\,f(y)=-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2xy}-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+3x=c.

$$

\displaystyle Q(t) = α(1 - \frac{t}{70}) + β(1 - \frac{t}{70})^{3}
$$
where $α$ and $β$ are constants, what is the value of $α + β$?

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question.

A saline reservoir for a medical research lab can hold up to $190\,\text{gal}$ of solution. Initially, it contains $50\,\text{gal}$ of saline solution with $20\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A more concentrated saline solution with concentration $1.2\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $1.2\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.2\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.2\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =18\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $50\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=50+15t-10t=5(10+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(10+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{10+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =18-\frac{2Q}{10+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q=18.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(10+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|10+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(10+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(10+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q) & =(10+t)^{2}\cdot 18 \\ (10+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(10+t)Q & =18(10+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2}) & =18(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 18(10+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(10+t)^{2} & =18\cdot \frac{1}{3}(10+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =6(10+t)+\frac{C}{(10+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 6(10+0)+\frac{C}{(10+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 60+\frac{C}{(10)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{(10)^{2}} & =-40 \\ C & =-40(10)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =6(10+t)-\frac{40(10)^{2}}{(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =6(10+t)-40{\left(\frac{10}{10+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $190\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=190$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =190 \\ 50+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =190 \\ 50+5{t}_{o} & =190 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =140 \\ {t}_{o} & =28\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(28) & =6(10+28)-40{\left(\frac{10}{10+28}\right)}^{2} \\  & =228-40{\left(\frac{10}{38}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈225.2\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now integrate and evaluate:

$$

Work on an interval where $\sin x\cos x\ne 0$.

Split the fraction and cancel common factors in each term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sin^{3}x-\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}
&=\frac{\sin^{3}x}{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}-\frac{\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x} \\
&=\frac{\sin x}{\cos^{2}x}-\frac{\cos x}{\sin^{2}x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the reciprocal and quotient definitions to recognize the derivative pairs:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sin x}{\cos^{2}x}&=\frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\sec x\tan x, \\
\frac{\cos x}{\sin^{2}x}&=\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\csc x\cot x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \frac{\sin^{3}x-\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}\,\mathrm{d}x
&=\int (\sec x\tan x-\csc x\cot x)\,\mathrm{d}x \\
&=\sec x-(-\csc x)+C \\
&=\sec x+\csc x+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations hold on the stated interval. Differentiating $\sec x+\csc x$ recovers $\sec x\tan x-\csc x\cot x$, which equals the original integrand there.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{-\sin^{3} x-2\cos^{3} x}{\sin^{2} x\cos^{2} x} \\
&=-\frac{\sin^{3} x}{\sin^{2} x\cos^{2} x}-2\frac{\cos^{3} x}{\sin^{2} x\cos^{2} x} \\
&=-\frac{\sin x}{\cos^{2} x}-2\frac{\cos x}{\sin^{2} x}
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the reciprocal and quotient definitions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sin x}{\cos^{2} x}&=\frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\sec x\tan x \\
\frac{\cos x}{\sin^{2} x}&=\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\csc x\cot x
\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand is therefore $-\sec x\tan x-2\csc x\cot x$. These cancellations hold on the stated interval.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int (\sec x\tan x)\,\mathrm{d}x&=\sec x+C. \\
\int (\csc x\cot x)\,\mathrm{d}x&=-\csc x+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int (-\sec x\tan x-2\csc x\cot x)\,\mathrm{d}x \\
&=-\int (\sec x\tan x)\,\mathrm{d}x-2\int (\csc x\cot x)\,\mathrm{d}x \\
&=-(\sec x)-2(-\csc x)+C \\

\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x,y)=(1-x)(y-2)^{2}$. The slope at $(x,y)$ is $f(x,y)$. A factor is zero on $x=1$ or $y=2$, so these are the zero-slope lines.

![Zero-slope lines dividing the plane into four open regions.](images/fc/fc16b1876053de0deeaa0c5d085a13975ca2883ad29bffc764cc7e4fc2064d9a.png)

Away from these lines, each factor has a fixed sign throughout each open region. Multiply the factor signs to determine the slope sign. The squared factor is strictly positive on both sides of $y=2$; it is zero on the line. Crossing this line does not reverse the sign.

| Region | $(1-x)$ | $(y-2)^{2}$ | $f(x,y)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x<1$, $y>2$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x>1$, $y>2$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |
| $x<1$, $y<2$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x>1$, $y<2$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

![Signs of the slope in all four open regions.](images/64/646e6b1237fb596521d8c6f0ec5e8df7027d238191021a1f7095726c0f080a99.png)

- Statement 1: for $x<1$ and $y>2$, the slope is positive. The statement is **true**.
- Statement 2: for $x<1$ and $y<2$, the slope is positive. The statement is **false**.
- Statement 3: for $x>1$ and $y<2$, the slope is negative. The statement is **false**.

“None of the above” is **false** because at least one ordinary statement is true.

The strict inequalities exclude the zero-slope lines; the slope is zero on those lines.

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 2y = 2e^{-2x}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y I(x) \right) = I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = 2$ and $Q(x) = 2e^{-2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = e^{2x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x} \\ {e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2{e}^{2x}\cdot y & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y I(x)\right){:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{2x}) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the general solution of the following differential equation using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac {3} {x} y = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}, \qquad x \gt 0.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = \dfrac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = x^3$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3}) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm d x = uv - \int u' v\,\textrm d x
$$

Let $u = x, u' = 1, v' = \cos x,$ and $v = \sin x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the following initial value problem using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 3x^2y = 9x^2, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x),
$$

with $P(x) = 3x^2$ and $Q(x) = 9x^2.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x) = e^{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot 9{x}^{2} \\ {e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot y & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}}) & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u = x^3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}})\text{d}x & =\int 9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =\int 3{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{{x}^{3}}+C \\ y & =3+C{e}^{-{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0) = 1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3+C{e}^{-{0}^{3}} \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = 3 - 2e^{-x^3}.
$$

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)$:
$\frac{dy}{dx} + y = \cos x$
Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x)) = I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

The equation is in standard form with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=\cos x$. An integrating factor is
$$
I(x)=e^{\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^x.
$$
Multiplying through by $e^x$ and using the product rule gives
$$
e^xy'+e^xy=e^x\cos x,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(ye^x)=e^x\cos x.
$$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y=3,\hspace{2em}x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below:

$\hspace{1em}$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\hspace{1em}$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

For $x>0$, an integrating factor is
$$
I(x)=e^{\int(2/x)\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{2\ln x}=x^2.
$$
Multiplying by $x^2$ and integrating gives
$$
(x^2y)'=3x^2,\qquad x^2y=x^3+C,\qquad y=x+\frac{C}{x^2}.
$$
Differentiation gives $y'+2y/x=3$, as required.

Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=1,\hspace{2em}y(0)=-3
$$

Select the correct options below.

$\hspace{1em}$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\hspace{1em}$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

An integrating factor is $I(x)=e^x$. Thus
$$
(e^xy)'=e^x,\qquad e^xy=e^x+C,\qquad y=1+Ce^{-x}.
$$
The initial condition gives $-3=1+C$, so $C=-4$. Therefore
$$
y(x)=1-4e^{-x}=1-\frac4{e^x}.
$$
This satisfies both $y'+y=1$ and $y(0)=-3$.

Consider the differential equation

$$
2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=3x.
$$

Select the correct options below.
$\hspace{1em}$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\hspace{1em}$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

First divide by $2$:
$$
y'+\frac12y=\frac32x.
$$
An integrating factor is $I(x)=e^{x/2}$. Integration by parts gives
$$
(ye^{x/2})'=\frac32xe^{x/2},\qquad ye^{x/2}=3(x-2)e^{x/2}+C.
$$
Hence
$$
y=3(x-2)+Ce^{-x/2}.
$$
Substitution verifies $2y'+y=3x$.

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y={x}^{2}{e}^{2x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.
$\hspace{1em}$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\hspace{1em}$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

An integrating factor is $I(x)=e^{-2x}$. Multiplying and integrating gives
$$
(ye^{-2x})'=x^2,\qquad ye^{-2x}=\frac{x^3}{3}+C.
$$
Therefore
$$
y=\frac{x^3e^{2x}}3+Ce^{2x}.
$$
Differentiating verifies $y'-2y=x^2e^{2x}$.

Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}\cdot y=x,\,y(0)=1
$$

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{x}{2}$ and $Q(x)=x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (x/2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot y & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}) & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4})\text{d}x & =\int x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =\int 2{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}+C \\ y & =2+C{e}^{-{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =2+C{e}^{-{0}^{2}/4} \\ 1 & =2+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2-{e}^{-{x}^{2}/4}.
$$

Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=4{x}^{2},\,y(1)=2
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

The first step is to write the equation in standard form,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)\,.
$$

In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y & =4{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x}(x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot 4{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\cdot y & =4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot 4x \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & ={x}^{4}+C \\ y & ={x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={1}^{2}+\frac{C}{{1}^{2}} \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)$:

Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x)) = I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

Here $P(x)=2x$, so an integrating factor is

Multiplication by $I(x)$ gives the exact derivative

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
x\frac{dy}{dx}+xy={x}^{2}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y=x.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+y) & ={e}^{x}\cdot x \\ {e}^{x}\frac{dy}{dx}+{e}^{x}y & ={e}^{x}\cdot x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot x\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}+xy={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,x>0
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y) & =x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ x\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(yx) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{2}y={x}^{3}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

$$

$$

with $P(x)=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{3}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1/2)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-x/2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{2}y) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3} \\ {e}^{-x/2}\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot y & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{-x/2}) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and $v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{2} & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2y}{x}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}},\,y(\pi )=0
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}.$ 

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\cdot y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(\pi )=0$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+C}{{\pi }^{2}} \\ 0 & =\frac{C}{{\pi }^{2}} \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0,\,y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y) & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ yx & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+C}{\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\ 1 & =\frac{2C}{\pi } \\ C & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2})}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi -2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x)$:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-2y=\sin x
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

The equation is already in standard form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$, with $P(x)=-2$ and $Q(x)=\sin x$. An integrating factor is

$$
I(x)=e^{\int -2\,dx}=e^{-2x}.
$$

Multiplying every term by $e^{-2x}$ gives

$$
e^{-2x}\frac{dy}{dx}-2e^{-2x}y=e^{-2x}\sin x.
$$

By the product rule, the left side is $\frac{d}{dx}(ye^{-2x})$. Thus the required equation is

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{-2x}\right)=e^{-2x}\sin x.
$$

The negative sign in $P(x)$ remains in the exponent. The right side must also be multiplied by the integrating factor.

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x)$:

$$
x\frac{dy}{dx}+y=xy+\cos x,\qquad x>0
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

Collect the $y$-terms on the left, then divide every term by $x>0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x\frac{dy}{dx}+(1-x)y&=\cos x\\
\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{1}{x}-1\right)y&=\frac{\cos x}{x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $P(x)=1/x-1$ and $Q(x)=\cos x/x$. Integrate both terms of $P(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I(x)&=e^{\int (1/x-1)\,dx}\\
&=e^{\ln x-x}\\
&=xe^{-x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply the standard-form equation by $xe^{-x}$:

$$
xe^{-x}\frac{dy}{dx}+(1-x)e^{-x}y=e^{-x}\cos x.
$$

Since $(xe^{-x})'=(1-x)e^{-x}$, the left side is the derivative of $yxe^{-x}$. Hence,

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\left(yxe^{-x}\right)=e^{-x}\cos x.
$$

Both collecting the $y$-terms and dividing the right side by $x$ are needed before applying the integrating factor.

Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{6x+11y}{\sqrt{y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{2y\sqrt{y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{6x+11y}{\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(6x+11y)\cdot \sqrt{y}-(6x+11y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y})}{{(\sqrt{y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(11\cdot \sqrt{y}-(6x+11y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}})}{y} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{22y-(6x+11y)}{2\sqrt{y}}\right)}{y} \\  & =\frac{11y-6x}{2y\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=11y-6x.
$$
For the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,3).$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}))) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(x{y}^{2})}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,3)} & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{1+{1}^{2}\cdot {3}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{9}{1+81} \\  & =\frac{9}{82}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(1) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}) & =2\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4})+8{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-8\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{3}+8{y}^{2}\cdot 2x-8\cdot 2x \\  & =8{x}^{3}+16x{y}^{2}-16x\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x}-y{z}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{z}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})-{z}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =x{y}^{x-1}-{z}^{3}\cdot (1) \\  & =x{y}^{x-1}-{z}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3y-2x}{7y-6x}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{(7y-6x)^{2}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{3y-2x}{7y-6x}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y-2x)\cdot (7y-6x)-(3y-2x)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(7y-6x)}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (7y-6x)-(3y-2x)\cdot (-6)}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-14y+12x+18y-12x}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4y}{(7y-6x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=4y.
$$

Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y))\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot 1}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)){e}^{x+y}}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y).
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))) \\  & =x((1)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))\end{aligned}

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$

$$

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1):$

The substitution $z=y^m$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}}
$$

into an equation of the form $z'(x) + P(x)z(x) = Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = x^3, \qquad q(x) = 1, \qquad n=-\dfrac12.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
y^{1/2} \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y^{3/2}= 1.\qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = \dfrac{3}{2}y^{1/2} \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^{1/2}\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(\ast)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + x^3\,z = 1
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{3}{2}x^3z = \dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad q(x) = x^2, \qquad n=-1.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by $y^{-1},$ and we get

$$
y \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{x}= x^2.
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{1}{x}z  = x^2
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{2}{x} z
		=2x^2
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2{x}^{2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =2{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2}) & =2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{2} & =\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{2{x}^{5}+C}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5C_1.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z=y^{2}.$ This results in the general solution

$$
y^{ 2} =\dfrac{2x^5 + C}{5x^2}.
$$

For real solutions, require $x\ne0$ and $2x^5+C>0$. The implicit relation retains both signs $y=\pm\sqrt{(2x^5+C)/(5x^2)}$. The original equation is undefined at $y=0$.

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n,
$$

where $n$ is a real number.

$$
y' + x^2y = e^x y^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) = e^x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation II is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = -xy^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) =-x, \qquad n=3.
$$

Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-{e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{x} & =-{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{C-{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use intervals where $C-e^{2x}\ne0$. The family displayed in the choices is nonzero. The original equation also admits $y=0$, which was excluded when dividing by a power of $y$.

Find the general **nonzero real** solution to the differential equation

$$
x^2\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=y^4-xy.
$$

Work on an interval with $x\ne0$ where the solution is finite. Interpret cube roots as real cube roots.

For $x\ne0$, write the equation in Bernoulli form:

$$
y'+\frac1x y=\frac1{x^2}y^4.
$$
We seek the nonzero real solutions, so divide by $y^4$ and set $z=y^{-3}$. The chain rule gives $z'=-3y^{-4}y'$, hence

$$
z'-\frac3x z=-\frac3{x^2}.
$$
On any interval avoiding $x=0$, an integrating factor is $I(x)=x^{-3}$, because $I'/I=-3/x$. Multiplying and integrating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x^{-3}z)'&=-3x^{-5},\\
x^{-3}z&=\frac3{4x^4}+K,\\
z&=\frac3{4x}+Kx^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
Now substitute $z=y^{-3}$ and absorb the factor $4$ into the arbitrary constant, writing $C=4K$:

$$
y^3=\frac{4x}{3+Cx^4},\qquad
\boxed{y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{4x}{3+Cx^4}}}.
$$
The cube root is the **real** cube root, so its argument may be negative. Use intervals with $x\ne0$ and $3+Cx^4\ne0$; on these intervals the family is real, finite and nonzero. The invertible substitution $z=y^{-3}$ recovers every nonzero solution there.

To verify the result without imposing a positive branch, put $g(x)=4x/(3+Cx^4)$. Since $y^3=g(x)\ne0$, implicit differentiation gives $y'=yg'/(3g)$, and

$$
x^2y'-y^4+xy
=y\left(\frac{x^2g'}{3g}-g+x\right)=0.
$$
The original equation also admits the equilibrium solution $y=0$. It is excluded only by the question's explicit **nonzero** condition; it was lost when dividing by $y^4$ and must be checked separately.

$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$

$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.

$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$

$$

Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy.
$$

First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{{y}^{-1}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x}\,⇒\,y=\frac{3x}{C-{x}^{3}}\,.
$$

Use intervals with $x\ne0$ and $C-x^3\ne0$. The original equation also admits $y=0$, outside the requested nonzero family.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.
$$

$$

This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

$$

$$

Here $p(x)=1/x$, $q(x)=2/x^2$, and $n=-\tfrac12$. Multiply by $\sqrt y$:

$$
y^{1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y^{3/2}}{x}=\frac{2}{x^2}.
$$

Set $z=y^{1-n}=y^{3/2}>0$. The chain rule gives $z'=\tfrac32 y^{1/2}y'$, hence

$$

$$
I(x)=e^{\int 3/(2x)\,dx}=e^{(3/2)\ln x}=x^{3/2}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Finally, $z=y^{3/2}$, so raise the expression for $z$ to the power $2/3$:

$$
y=\frac{(6\sqrt x+C)^{2/3}}{x}.
$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(3\right)z=3 \cdot e^{x}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int 3\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{3 \cdot x}.$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{3 \cdot x}\,z\right)=3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{3 \cdot x}z=\frac{3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}}{4}+C.$$

Thus

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{4 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{4 \cdot C + 3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}}.$$

Find the exact solution of the equation $2^{x+1}=3.$

First, we take $\log_2$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{x+1} & =3 \\ {log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x+1}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x+1 = \log_2 \left( 3 \right).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ x & ={log}_{2}⁡(3)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x= \log_2 \left( 3 \right) - 1.$
Given that $3^{2x+3}=5,$ find the value of $x$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Taking $\log_3$ of both sides of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
   	3^{2x+3} 				&= 5 \\[3pt]
	\log_3 \left(3^{2x+3}\right)	&= \log_3 (5) \\[3pt]
	2x+3 					&= \log_3 (5) . \\[3pt]
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ 2x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}-3 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above expression using a calculator gives

$$
x \approx -0.768
$$

Now, since $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we have
